[Chapter 2](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/linear_algebra.html) of *Deep Learning* (Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville) is the spine for the linear algebra this workshop assumes, and the [prerequisites on the homepage](index.qmd#prerequisites) say what else to do before the session. Neither covers Tucker or CP at all. This page is where to go next.

## Linear algebra, to go deeper {#ref-linear-algebra}

Three books, in increasing order of how much numerical detail they make you look at. Any one of them covers everything sections 03 to 09 lean on.

- Strang, G. — [*Introduction to Linear Algebra*](https://math.mit.edu/~gs/linearalgebra/) — the accessible one.<br>
  <small>Author pages: [Gilbert Strang](https://math.mit.edu/~gs/)</small>
- Trefethen, L. N. & Bau, D. — [*Numerical Linear Algebra*](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/trefethen/text.html) — the one that takes SVD seriously.<br>
  <small>Author pages: [Nick Trefethen](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/trefethen/)</small>
- Golub, G. H. & Van Loan, C. F. — [*Matrix Computations*](https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/10678/matrix-computations) — the reference, for when something is numerically wrong.<br>
  <small>Author pages: [Gene Golub](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Golub/) · [Charles Van Loan](https://as.cornell.edu/people/charles-van-loan)</small>

## Tensors specifically {#ref-tensors}

The survey first, then the four papers the workshop's last three sections are built on — all of them readable, and three of them older than the field that now uses them.

- Kolda, T. G. & Bader, B. W. (2009). [*Tensor Decompositions and Applications*](https://doi.org/10.1137/07070111X), SIAM Review 51(3), 455–500 — the survey. If you read one thing after this workshop, it is this.<br>
  <small>Author pages: [Tamara Kolda](https://www.mathsci.ai/) · [Brett Bader](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=OJQ8pq0AAAAJ)</small>
- Tucker, L. R. (1966). [*Some mathematical notes on three-mode factor analysis*](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02289464), Psychometrika 31, 279–311 — section 10's decomposition, from the source.
- Carroll, J. D. & Chang, J.-J. (1970). [*Analysis of individual differences in multidimensional scaling via an N-way generalization of “Eckart-Young” decomposition*](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02310791), Psychometrika 35, 283–319 — CP, arrived at as a generalization of Eckart–Young. Discovered independently and twice — see Harshman below.
- Harshman, R. A. (1970). [*Foundations of the PARAFAC procedure*](https://www.psychology.uwo.ca/faculty/harshman/wpppfac0.pdf), UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 16, 1–84 — the same decomposition, reached from psychometrics rather than from Eckart–Young, and named PARAFAC. Hence “CP/PARAFAC”.<br>
  <small>Author pages: [Richard Harshman](https://psychology.uwo.ca/faculty/harshman/)</small>
- Eckart, C. & Young, G. (1936). [*The approximation of one matrix by another of lower rank*](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02288367), Psychometrika 1, 211–218 — the truncated SVD is the optimal low-rank approximation. This is the theorem underneath Tucker and CP both, and Appendix E is where optimal on the Frobenius norm stops being enough.

## Software {#ref-software}

The workshop writes CP and Tucker out with `numpy` first, so that what the library does is not a mystery. For real projects, use the library.

- [`tensorly`](https://tensorly.org) — the tensor library, used in section 10 and Appendix C — see its [Tucker](https://tensorly.org/stable/modules/generated/tensorly.decomposition.tucker.html) and [CP](https://tensorly.org/dev/modules/generated/tensorly.decomposition.CP.html) implementations.<br>
  <small>Author pages: [Jean Kossaifi](https://jeankossaifi.com/)</small>
